justification: No article in this set reports KCNC1 (Kv3.1) variants in epilepsy patients or families; the only human genetic reports concern Usher syndrome type IC (where no coding mutations were found, PMID 9041816), a social-disinhibition SNP association (PMID 25161819), and chromosomal mapping (PMID 8111118) — none of which address epilepsy. The epilepsy-relevant evidence is entirely biological/pharmacological: Kv3.1-containing channels are implicated in 4-aminopyridine-induced seizure-like activity and chronic epileptic reorganization in rats (PMID 17942314), and the antiepileptic levetiracetam suppresses Kv3.1-encoded delayed rectifier current (PMID 20065495), with Kv3.1 controlling fast spiking and action-potential repolarization in neurons (PMIDs 21750937, 22105078, 16595659). Notably, Kcnc1-null mice do not show increased spontaneous seizures (PMID 9037088), weakening even the animal-model case. Therefore the relationship is best described as Hypothesized, based on channel biology and excitability/antiepileptic-drug links, with some residual probability of Novel given the negative mouse phenotype and absence of any human epilepsy data.

justification: All of the provided literature concerns CHRNA1, the muscle-type nicotinic acetylcholine receptor alpha-1 subunit, in the context of congenital myasthenic syndromes, fetal akinesia deformation sequence/multiple pterygium syndrome, and autoimmune myasthenia gravis — disorders of the neuromuscular junction, not of the central nervous system. No article reports epilepsy, seizures, or any CNS excitability phenotype, and none provides variant, expression, or model data connecting CHRNA1 to epileptogenesis. The splicing, channel-gating, and thymic-expression studies cited are mechanistically relevant only to neuromuscular transmission and immune tolerance. A small residual probability for "Hypothesized" reflects only the generic biology of nicotinic receptor subunits (other, neuronal subunits being epilepsy genes), which is not supported by anything in this corpus. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel.

justification: No article in this set reports LRRTM2 sequence variants in ASD probands or families; mentions of autism in PMIDs 24587117, 21155806, 21424692 and 20519524 are background statements or concern NRXN1/NRXN2 variants rather than LRRTM2 itself. The only human genetic study, PMID 23326251, proposes LRRTM2 as a candidate within a multigene 5q31 microdeletion (which cannot isolate the gene) and explicitly found no relevant LRRTM2 point mutations after sequencing 330 ID/DD patients — a negative result, and for ID/DD rather than ASD. However, the biology is directly relevant: LRRTM2 is a postsynaptic adhesion molecule binding neurexins, which cooperates with neuroligins in glutamatergic synapse development (PMIDs 20519524, 24005312), placing it squarely in an ASD-implicated synaptic pathway. This supports a Hypothesized relationship rather than Existing or Established; a small residual probability is left for Existing given unexamined candidate-gene framing, and for Novel given the negative mutation screen.

justification: The only human genetic observation linking GRIA2 to autism is a single case report of a child with autism carrying a ~19 Mb interstitial 4q32-q34 deletion that removes GRIA2 (AMPA2) along with ~33 other genes including GLRB, GLRA3, NPY1R and NPY5R (PMID 15090072); such a multigenic CNV cannot single out GRIA2, and a similar 4q32 deletion was reported with intellectual disability/psychosis rather than autism (PMIDs 20358617, 22669415). No case-control, family-based or sequencing study of GRIA2 variants in ASD appears here; the GRIP1 autism association study concerns a different gene, although it implicates GluA2 trafficking biology (PMID 21383172), and post-mortem reports of reduced GluA2 with elevated GRIP in autistic cerebellum are expression-level, not variant-level, evidence (PMID 24380676). Remaining GRIA2 genetic papers address schizophrenia, lithium response, depression and motor neuron disease, which are irrelevant homologous-phenotype citations. Thus the evidence sits between a weak, non-definitive human genetic hint (Existing) and purely biological/expression plausibility (Hypothesized), with nothing approaching replicated causal proof.
